title: Those Who Realize will Know, Those Who Know will Realize
paragraphs: > Compositions admit of > No violation of the conventions in vogue; > Use of diction tested through tradition > Should inform the usage therein.
(Poruḷatikāram : Marapiyal, verse 92)
This verse emphasizes that words not breaching the established conventions must go into the making of a verse.
I am not adept in the grammar of poetry. I brought out, sixty years ago, a book of verses titled “It is No Poetry”, wherein I have openly admitted my verses being metreless.

I have presided at many poetic meets of eminent poets through years. And this is what I wrote as my presidential address in the poetic meet, on the theme ‘Freedom Fighters’ broadcast on the All India Radio, Tiruchi, in the year 1967.

> He in prison lived, and pulled the oilpress, > To drive away the Whites who ruled the land. > Many were killed before the prime of their lives. > He fought like a sword drawn from out of the sheath, > With no care for his life. > Of his glory to hear, > We are all arrayed here today. > > But to describe the greatness of all those > Who have their lives laid down for freedom, > I have neither the poetic ability acquired, > Nor the art of poetry learnt. > > Though my verses might poetic metre lack, > Guided as I was by the sole principle > That our land, language, honour and feelings > Should not go undefended, > I make poetic lines of my feelings, > That from my heart do gush forth, > To let those treacherous ones, > The turncoats of principles, gain awareness > I shall say this. > > Freedom was gained, > By the loss of so many lives, by the loss of so much blood! > After great loss and labour on earth, > Freedom, like purest gold, was earned.
> Can we throw it away? > Good is it to hand over this rose beautiful, > To a monkey wild? > Our freedom let us zealously guard, > Let us add glory to those freedom fighters.
Thus is the age of new poetry, an age when novelties like haiku are being composed.
To put it in other words, it is the age when words and sentences are juggled or lines broken and they are paraded as rhythmic poetry.

I do not claim that I am the one versed in prosody, and yet my verse portraits are no eyeless needles. I have the sense of pride to proclaim that my poems have remained the magnetic particles drawing even eyeless needles unto their fold. Here are a few examples:

> The world to be one with all lands united, > Mankind to be knit as one by human love- > Are the noble thoughts articulated by the poet. > > But even he, he as a poet did live > With his place name, Pūṅkuṉṟam, after his name. > And he was known as Kaṇiyaṉ Pūṅkuṉṟaṉār. > > When we contemplate this carefully > Doesn’t it strike as true > That even this man of eminence > Was bound by the love of his land?
Another poem:

> He was the lion of a Tamil with self-respect > Who wouldn’t bend > Even to kiss his toddling child; > Instead he would get the child lifted over his head > And go about fondling it. > > He was not used to looking down to the ground, > And he would plant a kiss > On the forehead of his love of moon-like face > With the face straight up.

> He wouldn’t bend like a question mark on the bed > But would lie down erect like an arrow with legs stretched out. > > Is he one with a backbone unbending? > Is his heart a field > Where the crop of obeisance never grows? > Amazed thus were many > With gaping mouths and fingers on the nose.
Yet another poem:

> There came a woman > Swinging like a jewelled chariot, > Walking on the verdant grass > Where the eggs of snow were being hatched. > > She was an adept in the flow of fruit-like Tamil words; > She was the elder sister of Kākkaippāṭiṉi Poṉmuṭiyār; > She sang the praises of > Atiyamāṉ Neṭumāṉañci and the munificent Pāri, > Cēramāṉ Māveṅkōvaṉ, > Kānapper tanta Vaḷuti > And the Cōḻa king Perunaṟkiḷḷi, > Thereby adding many a jewel to Tamil, > She is Avvai, the light of wisdom!
Another instance:

> Honour! That’s the lullaby my son listened to; > Death! That’s the sport he played; > I taught him the art of using lances > Even as he was a suckling; > > He turned a worthy son to his father > As aerial roots to a banyan tree; > > He rose against the foes in rage, > The foes with stunted minds like the goat’s tail, > Who dared to usurp our throne, > He flayed them and saw them routed > And he gave his life in the deed.
> He is now the ruler of fame winning. > Look not at my eyes raining tears! > Look at my heart in joy immersed!
One more of my poems:

> Such a joy she did not experience on her marriage; > Son’s birth too did not give her as much happiness. > > Look! there he lies dead > With a spear piercing his chest! > She saw this and her heart leapt in joy. > > O, I was about to pluck away my breasts that fed him > O, where is that wicked man who told me a blatant lie > (That he died with a spear on his back)? > Here is the sword! Where is the tongue of that man?

I keep dedicating at the feet of Mother Tamil such of these poetic portraits that are a blend of the sound of the sword’s sway and the music of the harp, and that have infused my fellow Tamils with a new vigour and a sense of amazement.

I might have strayed away from the established conventions of versification. But my mind has all along remained undistracted. The readers who have had a feel of the import of the blossoms of Tolkāppiyam presented so far by me would understand this truth. And those who have understood this will feel it in their heart of hearts.
